quotes.text: It's not built to stop hackers, it's designed to stop your own people from accidentally leaking sensitive data.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clarifies what DLP is actually for in one sentence.

quotes.text: Instead of blocking everything, it watches three things, what the data is, who's handling it and where it's going. Then it enforces rules automatically.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains the core DLP model in plain terms.

quotes.text: DLP is a governance program, not an IT project. You need business stakeholders in the room, legal compliance HR finance, people who understand how data actually flows.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Names the most common reason DLP deployments fail and how to avoid it.

quotes.text: Keep it simple, start with three to five labels. Public internal confidential, highly confidential, expand only after people have adopted the basics.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives concrete, actionable guidance on label design.

quotes.text: 58% of leaks are accidental. DLP isn't about punishing users. It's about catching honest mistakes before they become headlines.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Sums up the purpose of DLP in a memorable way.

takeaways: Most data leaks are accidental, so Microsoft Purview DLP focuses on catching honest mistakes by watching what the data is, who handles it and where it goes.
DLP covers Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, endpoints and Copilot, and each channel is a separate door that needs its own policy coverage.
Treat DLP as a governance program: keep sensitivity labels simple, start in simulation mode, use policy tips and only then turn enforcement on.
hook: Most data leaks are not attacks but honest mistakes by your own people. This episode explains to IT and security teams how Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention protects sensitive data across email, files, Teams chats, devices and Copilot, and how to roll it out without breaking legitimate workflows.
